Grasshoppers, Beef Heart, and Sticky Beans: Six Surprising Real Dishes

Quality checked lesson

Published 16 Sep 2026

Chapulines, anticuchos, natto, stinky tofu, mopane worms, and kitfo look strange to many first-time eaters, but each one is an everyday food with a clear reason behind the mix. Three simple questions explain them: where the food comes from, how people change it, and what the finished dish tastes like.

Text to type: Many surprising foods start with a simple idea: use what is around you, then change it with heat and strong seasoning. In Latin America, two street foods show this clearly. Chapulines are grasshoppers eaten in parts of Mexico and Central America. The name comes from Nahuatl, an old language of Mexico, and Spanish records from the early to mid-16th century already mention grasshoppers as food. Oaxaca is the main region, but they are also popular near Mexico City, Tepoztlán, Cuernavaca, and Puebla. The insect itself is the source; the change is toasting them and seasoning with garlic, lime juice, chilies, or salt. The result is a crunchy, salty, sour snack, or a filling for a large tortilla dish called a tlayuda. Anticuchos come from the Andes, especially Peru, and also Bolivia, Chile, and Ecuador. The most popular version uses beef heart. In colonial times, Spanish households valued organ cuts less, so these cheap cuts became common in street food, and today people across Peru eat anticuchos. The heart is marinated in vinegar and spices such as cumin, aji pepper, and garlic, then grilled on a skewer, often with a boiled potato at the end. The strong marinade and smoky grill change a cheap cut into something people line up for.

Check: Part 1: Latin America – chapulines and anticuchos

1. Why did beef heart become the usual meat for anticuchos in Peru?

Sample answer

In colonial times, Spanish households valued organ cuts less, so cheap cuts like beef heart went into street food, and anticuchos de corazón became the most popular version.

Text to type: In Asia, the surprise often comes not from the ingredient but from the change. Both natto and stinky tofu begin with soybeans, a very ordinary food, and both are fermented, which means bacteria or other tiny organisms slowly change the food over time. Fermentation creates the smell that shocks newcomers and the flavor that fans love. Natto is whole soybeans fermented with a bacterium called Bacillus subtilis var. natto. In eastern Japan, including Kanto, Tohoku, and Hokkaido, many people eat it for breakfast on rice with mustard, soy sauce, and spring onion. The change gives it a strong smell, a sticky texture with long strings, and a strong taste. Many call it an acquired taste, yet a 2009 survey found about 70 percent of respondents liked it. So a food that looks difficult is, for most people in its home region, simply a normal morning meal. Stinky tofu is Chinese fermented tofu, a famous night-market snack in Taiwan and common in many parts of China. A legend says Wang Zhihe made an early version in the Qing dynasty after leftover tofu fermented in a jar. People compare the smell to strong cheese or even garbage, but the taste is usually milder and savory. It can be steamed, stewed, or grilled, though fried stinky tofu is the night-market favorite, and fans say the smellier batches often taste better.

Text to type: In Africa, two dishes show a different kind of contrast: one is a wild insect turned into a shelf-stable food, and the other is fresh raw meat made rich with spice and butter. Mopane worms are large caterpillars of the moth Gonimbrasia belina, common in warmer southern Africa. They feed mainly on the leaves of the mopane tree, and they are an important source of protein in the region. After cleaning, people boil them with salt and then dry or smoke them. The change matters: drying turns a soft caterpillar into a crunchy snack that keeps for a long time, or it can be cooked again with onion, tomato, and spices. Because they keep well, they are traded across countries such as Botswana, Namibia, South Africa, and Zimbabwe. Kitfo is an Ethiopian dish from Gurage tradition, made of minced raw beef. Here the change is not heat but seasoning: the meat is mixed with mitmita, a hot chili spice powder, and niter kibbeh, a spiced clarified butter. When it is cooked lightly rare, it is called kitfo leb leb. It is often served with ayibe, a mild cheese, or gomen, cooked greens, together with injera flatbread or, among Gurage cooks, with kocho. Kitfo appears on special days such as the feast of Meskel, so the raw meat that surprises visitors is, for many Ethiopians, a celebration food.

1. What two things change mopane worms from a wild caterpillar into a food that can be traded?

Part 1: Latin America – chapulines and anticuchos

Many surprising foods start with a simple idea: use what is around you, then change it with heat and strong seasoning.

In Latin America, two street foods show this clearly.

Chapulines are grasshoppers eaten in parts of Mexico and Central America.

The name comes from Nahuatl, an old language of Mexico, and Spanish records from the early to mid-16th century already mention grasshoppers as food.

Oaxaca is the main region, but they are also popular near Mexico City, Tepoztlán, Cuernavaca, and Puebla.

The insect itself is the source; the change is toasting them and seasoning with garlic, lime juice, chilies, or salt.

The result is a crunchy, salty, sour snack, or a filling for a large tortilla dish called a tlayuda.

Anticuchos come from the Andes, especially Peru, and also Bolivia, Chile, and Ecuador.

The most popular version uses beef heart.

In colonial times, Spanish households valued organ cuts less, so these cheap cuts became common in street food, and today people across Peru eat anticuchos.

The heart is marinated in vinegar and spices such as cumin, aji pepper, and garlic, then grilled on a skewer, often with a boiled potato at the end.

The strong marinade and smoky grill change a cheap cut into something people line up for.

Reading

Part 2: Asia – natto and stinky tofu

In Asia, the surprise often comes not from the ingredient but from the change.

Both natto and stinky tofu begin with soybeans, a very ordinary food, and both are fermented, which means bacteria or other tiny organisms slowly change the food over time.

Fermentation creates the smell that shocks newcomers and the flavor that fans love.

Natto is whole soybeans fermented with a bacterium called Bacillus subtilis var.

natto.

In eastern Japan, including Kanto, Tohoku, and Hokkaido, many people eat it for breakfast on rice with mustard, soy sauce, and spring onion.

The change gives it a strong smell, a sticky texture with long strings, and a strong taste.

Many call it an acquired taste, yet a 2009 survey found about 70 percent of respondents liked it.

So a food that looks difficult is, for most people in its home region, simply a normal morning meal.

Stinky tofu is Chinese fermented tofu, a famous night-market snack in Taiwan and common in many parts of China.

A legend says Wang Zhihe made an early version in the Qing dynasty after leftover tofu fermented in a jar.

People compare the smell to strong cheese or even garbage, but the taste is usually milder and savory.

It can be steamed, stewed, or grilled, though fried stinky tofu is the night-market favorite, and fans say the smellier batches often taste better.

Part 3: Africa – mopane worms and kitfo

In Africa, two dishes show a different kind of contrast: one is a wild insect turned into a shelf-stable food, and the other is fresh raw meat made rich with spice and butter.

Mopane worms are large caterpillars of the moth Gonimbrasia belina, common in warmer southern Africa.

They feed mainly on the leaves of the mopane tree, and they are an important source of protein in the region.

After cleaning, people boil them with salt and then dry or smoke them.

The change matters: drying turns a soft caterpillar into a crunchy snack that keeps for a long time, or it can be cooked again with onion, tomato, and spices.

Because they keep well, they are traded across countries such as Botswana, Namibia, South Africa, and Zimbabwe.

Kitfo is an Ethiopian dish from Gurage tradition, made of minced raw beef.

Here the change is not heat but seasoning: the meat is mixed with mitmita, a hot chili spice powder, and niter kibbeh, a spiced clarified butter.

When it is cooked lightly rare, it is called kitfo leb leb.

It is often served with ayibe, a mild cheese, or gomen, cooked greens, together with injera flatbread or, among Gurage cooks, with kocho.

Kitfo appears on special days such as the feast of Meskel, so the raw meat that surprises visitors is, for many Ethiopians, a celebration food.
